title: Design Uber
problem: A quarter of a million driver positions a second must be searchable by location, and each ride must go to exactly one driver even when two dispatchers race.
summary: Driver positions stream into an in-memory grid of H3 or geohash cells that answers nearby-driver queries; a dispatcher ranks candidates by road ETA and offers trips one driver at a time; a conditional transaction assigns exactly one; surge and ETA run as separate services.
catTip: Four hundred location pings arrive for every ride anyone actually books. I let the pings pile up in hexagonal baskets and forget the old ones, and I save my one careful transaction for the moment a driver says yes.

recall.q: A quarter of a million driver positions a second arrive, but only six hundred ride requests. What does that ratio tell you about where to spend durability and consistency?
recall.a: Spend none on positions: each sample supersedes the last, so they go to an in-memory grid index of H3 or geohash cells plus an append-only log, and losing one costs nothing. Spend all of it on the match: the trip and driver rows change state in one conditional transaction on one shard so exactly one driver is assigned, and the rider's request carries an idempotency key.

guide.breaks: Writing every driver position to a database drowns it in a quarter of a million writes a second that are obsolete in four seconds, and matching without a conditional transaction sends two cars to one rider the first time a dispatcher retries.
guide.tradeoffs: Keeping positions only in memory means a crashed index node forgets a city for a few seconds, sharding trips and drivers by city makes cross-city trips a special case, and offering one driver at a time makes riders wait through declines.
guide.explainSimply: Picture a taxi rank with a whiteboard and a ledger. Drivers shout where they are and the dispatcher scribbles it on the whiteboard, wiping old scribbles as new shouts arrive. When a fare comes in, the dispatcher radios one driver at a time, and only when one says yes writes the fare in the ledger, in ink, against that driver.
guide.hint: Ask which data can be regenerated in four seconds and which data is money, and which shard key lets the trip and the driver change together.

meow: Pings in hex baskets, old ones forgotten. One driver, one trip, one transaction. Surge is someone else's whiskers. Meow.

quiz.prompt: Two dispatch workers, one of them retrying after a timeout, offer two different trips to the same idle driver, and the driver taps accept on both offers within a second. What guarantees the driver ends up with exactly one trip?
options: The geo index removes the driver from its cell the moment the first offer is sent, so the second worker never sees them as a candidate

A conditional transaction on one shard: the driver row flips from available to assigned only if it is still available, and the trip row flips from requested to matched in the same transaction; the second accept changes zero rows and gets 409
The driver app disables the accept button after the first tap, so the second accept is never sent
A distributed lock on the rider id held by the dispatch worker for the length of the offer
quiz.explanation: Only the conditional update on the driver's own state, committed together with the trip's transition, is authoritative under a race. The geo index option is the strongest distractor: it is a lossy in-memory cache that both workers may have read before either offer was sent, and it was never the source of truth for assignment.

quiz.prompt: An airport taxi rank puts 3,000 idle drivers inside one 0.74 km² H3 cell. A rider two kilometres away requests a ride and dispatch pulls every driver in the covering cells for ETA ranking. What breaks, and what is the right fix?
options: Replace the grid with a quadtree, which splits dense cells automatically as drivers arrive
The ETA ranker is handed thousands of candidates; because H3 cells nest, index the hot cell's drivers at a finer resolution too, query the finer level first and cap the candidates passed to ranking
Widen the search radius so that candidates from other cells dilute the dense one
Shard the hot cell's driver set across more index machines by driver id
quiz.explanation: The grid stays O(1) per position update and the nested resolution gives density adaptivity only where it is needed. The quadtree is the strongest distractor: it would adapt to density, but it pays for splits and merges on every one of 250k position writes a second, which is the reason the design chose a grid in the first place.

cards.q: Problem: a million drivers report their position every 4 s, and "which drivers are within 2 km" must answer in milliseconds. Decision and why?
cards.a: An in-memory grid index: map each position to an H3 (or geohash or S2) cell, keep a hash map from cell to drivers sharded by region, and answer a query by reading the cells in the k-ring around the pickup and filtering by distance. A grid makes a move one delete and one insert, where a quadtree would split or merge on every one of 250k writes a second; H3 is preferred because its hexagons have one neighbour distance, nest across 16 resolutions for hot cells like airports, and are the same cells surge uses. Positions are never written to a database: the next sample replaces them in 4 s.

cards.q: Problem: a driver taps accept just as the offer expires, or two dispatchers race for the same driver, and two cars must never go to one rider. Decision and why?
cards.a: Shard trips and drivers by city so the two rows share a shard, then make the match one transaction with two conditional updates: the driver flips available to assigned only if still available and the trip flips requested to matched only if still requested; zero rows changed means 409 and re-dispatch, and a late accept is rejected by its expired offer id. Choose the shard key so the invariant lives on one shard; reach for a saga or a globally consistent store only when cross-region trips make that impossible, which is the trade Uber describes making in its own rebuild.

glossary.note: A routing engine's road-graph travel time, corrected by a model trained on actual trips; the hot read path of a ride-hailing design.

sources.title: Uber Engineering, "H3: Uber's Hexagonal Hierarchical Spatial Index" (27 June 2018)
sources.supports: hexagons minimise the quantisation error of users moving through a city; a hexagon has one neighbour distance where a square has two and a triangle three; sixteen resolutions with each child one seventh of the parent's area; Uber buckets marketplace events into hexagons and calculates surge pricing by measuring supply and demand in hexagons

sources.title: H3 documentation, "Tables of cell statistics across resolutions"
sources.supports: 16 resolutions (0 to 15); average hexagon area 0.737 km² at resolution 8, 0.105 km² at resolution 9 and 0.015 km² at resolution 10; average edge length about 0.53 km at resolution 8 and 0.20 km at resolution 9

sources.title: Uber Engineering, "Building Uber's Fulfillment Platform for Planet-Scale using Google Cloud Spanner"
sources.supports: the previous stack used Ringpop application-level sharding with an in-memory serial queue, an AP design that traded consistency for availability; saga-based multi-entity writes could leave entities inconsistent and needed manual repair; consistency became a primary evaluation criterion; the move to Cloud Spanner; billions of database transactions a day and billions of trips a month

sources.title: Uber Engineering, "DeepETA: How Uber Predicts Arrival Times Using Deep Learning"
sources.supports: the routing engine estimates a sum of segment traversal times along the best path using map data and real-time traffic; machine learning predicts the residual between the routing-engine ETA and observed outcomes (ETA post-processing); the model must return within a few milliseconds; it is the highest-QPS model at Uber

sources.title: High Scalability, "How Uber Scales Their Real-time Market Platform" (14 September 2015)
sources.supports: drivers send a location update every 4 seconds; Google S2 level-12 cells (about 3 to 6 km²) used as the sharding key for supply, with the circle around a rider covered by cells; DISCO ranks candidates by road-based ETA before offering a trip; ringpop as a consistent hash ring with SWIM gossip, an AP system; a summary of a conference talk, so secondary

sources.title: Uber, "How surge pricing works"
sources.supports: surge applies when so many people request rides that there are not enough cars; it is specific to areas within a city and updates in real time; it appears as a multiplier, an additional surge amount or an upfront fare depending on the city

sources.title: S2 Geometry, "S2 Cell Statistics"
sources.supports: 31 levels (0 to 30); level-12 cells range from 3.04 to 6.38 km² with an average of 5.07 km²

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Geohash"
sources.supports: a 6-character geohash has an error of about ±0.61 km and a 7-character one about ±76 m (so a 6-character cell is roughly 1.2 km by 0.6 km); a longer shared prefix means spatially closer, but two close points on either side of a cell boundary (notably the Equator or Greenwich meridian) may share no prefix, so neighbours must be queried explicitly
